fields.explanation: The complete source first chooses a vertex v of degree n-2 and its unique nonneighbor u. For the original six-vertex graph, use v=5 and u=0. Then N(v)={1,2,3,4}, N(u)={3,4}, and the later nonneighbors indexed v_(k+1),...,v_(n-2) are exactly {1,2}; the distinguished v=5 is not among them. Vertex 1 has common neighbor 3 with u, and vertex 2 has common neighbor 4 with u. Neither 3 nor 4 meets both: edge 32 is absent and edge 41 is absent. All degrees are at most 4, v has degree 4, and every nonadjacent pair has a common neighbor, so every ambient source hypothesis holds. The invalid step exchanges the quantifiers: for each required vertex there is a suitable neighbor, but no single suitable neighbor works for both. The original primary graph is preserved. The archived P4 supporting example violates the source common-neighbor hypothesis and is not evidence for this record. The five-vertex secondary discussion and the old blind-source caveat are also not used. This refutes the intermediate WLOG choice, not the final edge lower bound.
fields.flaw: After selecting v=5 and its unique nonneighbor u=0, the source requires a single neighbor of u adjacent to all residual vertices v_(k+1),...,v_(n-2). Here those residual vertices are {1,2}, not the distinguished vertex 5. Neighbor 3 misses 2 and neighbor 4 misses 1, so the asserted common choice does not exist.
fields.problem: If $G$ is a $(n,m)$ graph such that $\Delta(G)=n-2$ and any two non-adjacent vertices have a common neighbour, then $m\geq 2n-4.$
fields.source_context:
0001 | Let $G$ be a graph of order $n$ and size $m$ such that $\Delta(G)=n-2$ and any two non-adjacent vertices have a common neighbour.  Show that $m\geq 2n-4.$
0002 | 
0003 | Kindly advise on my proof. Thank you.
0004 | 
0005 | Let $v\in G$ such that $v$ is adjacent to$ v_1,..., v_{n-2}$ and not adjacent to $u.$
0006 | 
0007 | Then $\sum_{g\in G} \text{deg}(g) \geq  (n-2)+(n-2) = 2n-4.$ 
0008 | 
0009 | Now suppose $u$ is adjacent to $v_1,...,v_k$ and not adjacent to $v_{k+1},..., v_{n-2}.$
0010 | Then $\sum_{g\in G} \text{deg}(g)$ will increase by at least $k+k=2k.$
0011 | 
0012 | Given $v_i(i=k+1,..., n-2), $ by assumption in the problem, there exists $v_j(j = 1,..., k)$ such that $v_j$  is adjacent to $v_i.$ We can assume $v_1$ will be adjacent to all $v_i(i=k+1,...,n-2).$
0013 | 
0014 | Then $\sum_{g\in G} \text{deg}(g)$ will increase by at least $n-2-k + n-2-k = 2n-4-2k.$
0015 | 
0016 | Hence, $2m = \sum_{g\in G} \text{deg}(g)\geq 2n-4-2k+2k+2n -4 = 4n -8.$
fields.witness: Use V={0,1,2,3,4,5} and E={03,04,13,15,24,25,34,35,45}. Degrees are[2,2,2,4,4,4], and every nonadjacent pair has a common neighbor. Set the source distinguished vertex v=5 and its unique nonneighbor u=0. Label v1=3,v2=4,v3=1,v4=2, so k=2. The residual vertices indexed i=k+1,...,n-2 are1 and2, excluding distinguished v=5. Candidate v1=3 is adjacent to1 but misses2; candidate v2=4 is adjacent to2 but misses1. Therefore neither neighbor of u covers all residual v_i. This valid six-vertex witness, with all original hypotheses, is exactly the selected Lean statement.
